other_side: Zitron's most recent long piece borrows Adam Curtis's idea of hypernormalisation: an industry and its fans constructing a simpler, reassuring story and managing appearances rather than facing what the numbers say. The shared context repository at the heart of NLW's sprint is, in his telling, exactly the trap: models that tell every user their idea is genius let people feel productive while endlessly prompting 'an ever-growing system (like a Wiki of your work)' that produces the look of productivity and very little value. He also points out that after three years and hundreds of billions of dollars there is no productivity payoff visible at national scale, and that the usual answer to 'what does AI change?' is still 'coding' plus a user count.
truth_beneath: The variable both men orbit is whether collaborative context makes agents more useful or merely more visible. Both accept as fact that most knowledge work is coordination rather than solo creation, that Anthropic, OpenClaw and Y Combinator are all now building shared-session tools, and that the aggregate productivity statistics remain unmoved. The empirical question that will resolve is whether shared agents change team output, and the observable is Anthropic's own claim that nearly two thirds of its product team's code now comes from a shared agent: either that figure is reproduced by unrelated firms within a year or it stays an in-house anecdote. The worldview residue is whether 'work about work' is waste to be automated or the social fabric of a job. NLW is vindicated if outside teams report shipped work, not sessions opened; Zitron if shared repositories become a new place to tinker. Both are polemicists with incentives, one bullish and anti-doom, the other bubble-certain and anti-hype, and they agree the present-tense evidence is thin. Watch for a non-lab company publishing that sixty-five per cent figure.
